"Pan" as a verb has three distinct, unrelated meanings. Each one is used in a completely different situation. Think of them as three separate words that just happen to be spelled the same.
Meaning 1: To Search for Gold (or Something Valuable) by Washing Material in a Pan

This is the oldest meaning. Imagine you are standing in a river during the Gold Rush. You scoop up a heap of wet sand and gravel from the riverbed into a shallow metal dish (called a pan). You then swirl it around with water so that the lighter sand and mud wash away over the rim, leaving only the heavy stuff — hopefully, flakes or nuggets of gold — sitting at the bottom.

That entire act of sifting and washing to find something valuable is called panning.

Examples:

  • Miners panned the river for gold.
  • She spent the afternoon panning for gemstones.

Today, the meaning has stretched slightly beyond gold mining. You can use "pan" to describe any careful sifting through a large amount of material to find something worth keeping — though this extended use is less common.

The Phrasal Verb: "Pan out"

This grows directly out of the gold-mining meaning above. When you panned for gold, sometimes you found gold (success!) and sometimes you didn't (failure). So "pan out" came to mean to turn out well, to succeed, or to work out as hoped.

Examples:

  • The business idea didn't pan out the way we expected. (= It didn't succeed.)
  • Let's wait and see how things pan out. (= Let's wait and see how things develop/turn out.)
  • His plan panned out perfectly. (= His plan worked out successfully.)

This phrasal verb is extremely common in everyday speech, so it's worth knowing well. Note that it's very often used in the negative — "didn't pan out" — because people frequently use it to describe something that failed or fell short.
Meaning 2: To Move a Camera Horizontally

This is a term from filmmaking and photography. When a camera is fixed on a tripod or held steady, but is rotated smoothly from left to right (or right to left) — without moving its position — the camera is said to pan. The camera sweeps across a scene the way your eyes do when you turn your head to look from one side of a room to the other.

This is different from zooming (making something appear closer or farther) or tilting (moving the camera up or down). Panning is purely the side-to-side horizontal sweep.

Examples:

  • The director told the camera operator to pan left to catch the actor walking in.
  • The documentary panned slowly across the vast mountain range.
  • The camera panned right to reveal the crowd.

A single such movement is called a pan shot, and the act of doing it is simply panning. You'll hear this word constantly in filmmaking, video production, gaming (moving a map view sideways), and even in music software (adjusting audio left or right in a stereo field — though that last use is more technical).

If a critic, journalist, or reviewer pans something — a film, a book, a restaurant, a performance, a product — they are giving it a very harsh, strongly negative review. It's not mild disapproval. Panning means tearing it apart, declaring it bad or a failure.

Examples:

  • The critics panned the film on opening night. (= They gave it terrible reviews.)
  • Her debut novel was panned by every major publication.
  • The restaurant was panned online for its poor service and cold food.
  • The press panned the politician's speech as confused and unconvincing.

The subject doing the panning is almost always a critic, a reviewer, the media, or the public. The thing being panned is typically a creative work, a public performance, or anything that is being judged.
A Quick Summary of All Three

Pan (verb) has three meanings:

  1. To wash material (sand, gravel) in a pan to find something valuable, such as gold. Extended into the phrasal verb "pan out" = to succeed or to turn out in a certain way.
  2. To rotate a camera horizontally from side to side to capture a wide or moving scene.
  3. To criticize something harshly — to give a very bad review or judgement.

These three meanings are completely independent of one another. Context always makes it clear which one is being used — a sentence about critics points to Meaning 3, a sentence about cameras points to Meaning 2, and a sentence about rivers or rivers of success points to Meaning 1.
